import hashlib as _html_hashlib
import importlib.util as _html_importlib
import json as _html_json
import math as _html_math
import re as _html_re
from collections import Counter as _HtmlCounter
from html.parser import HTMLParser as _HTMLParser
from pathlib import Path as _HtmlPath

HTML_EVAL_DATASET = "bs-modeling-metadata/c4-en-html-with-metadata"
HTML_EVAL_REVISION = "d7fa66c5f9686a055f50dbdaeb0d8950209cf0f8"
HTML_EVAL_SPLIT = "train"
HTML_EVAL_VERSION = "html-extraction-family-evaluation-v1"
HTML_EVAL_ROOT = _HtmlPath("data/c4_en_html_evaluation")
HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR = HTML_EVAL_ROOT / "impl"
HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH = HTML_EVAL_ROOT / "raw_html.jsonl"
HTML_EVAL_MANIFEST_PATH = HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR / "selection_manifest.json"
HTML_EVAL_METRICS_PATH = HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR / "technique_metrics.json"
HTML_EVAL_DOCUMENT_METRICS_PATH = (
    HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR / "document_metrics.jsonl"
)
_HTML_EVAL_MAX_CHARS = 500_000
_HTML_EVAL_TOKEN = _html_re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9'’-]*")
_HTML_EVAL_BLOCK_TAGS = {
    "address",
    "article",
    "aside",
    "blockquote",
    "br",
    "dd",
    "div",
    "dl",
    "dt",
    "fieldset",
    "figcaption",
    "figure",
    "footer",
    "form",
    "h1",
    "h2",
    "h3",
    "h4",
    "h5",
    "h6",
    "header",
    "hr",
    "li",
    "main",
    "nav",
    "ol",
    "p",
    "pre",
    "section",
    "table",
    "td",
    "th",
    "tr",
    "ul",
}
_HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS = {"script", "style", "noscript", "template", "svg"}
_HTML_EVAL_LIBRARY_STATUS = {
    package: _html_importlib.find_spec(module) is not None
    for package, module in {
        "Trafilatura": "trafilatura",
        "jusText": "justext",
        "Inscriptis": "inscriptis",
        "Resiliparse": "resiliparse",
        "extruct": "extruct",
        "readability-lxml": "readability",
    }.items()
}

def _html_normalize(value):
    return _html_re.sub(r"\s+", " ", value or " ").strip()

def _html_tokens(value):
    return set(
        token.lower() for token in _HTML_EVAL_TOKEN.findall(value or "")
    )

def _html_overlap(candidate, reference):
    candidate_tokens = _html_tokens(candidate)
    reference_tokens = _html_tokens(reference)
    if not candidate_tokens or not reference_tokens:
        return 0.0
    return len(candidate_tokens & reference_tokens) / len(reference_tokens)

class _HtmlTextRenderer(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self, layout=False):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.parts = []
        self.layout = layout
        self.skip_depth = 0
        self.tag_count = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        self.tag_count += 1
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth == 0 and tag in _HTML_EVAL_BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.parts.append("\n" if self.layout else " ")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        self.tag_count += 1
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
        if self.skip_depth == 0 and tag in _HTML_EVAL_BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.parts.append("\n" if self.layout else " ")

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth == 0:
            self.parts.append(data)

    def render(self):
        value = "".join(self.parts)
        return (
            _html_re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", value).strip()
            if self.layout
            else _html_normalize(value)
        )

class _HtmlBlockCollector(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.blocks = []
        self.current = None
        self.link_depth = 0
        self.skip_depth = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a":
            self.link_depth += 1
        if tag in {
            "p",
            "li",
            "h1",
            "h2",
            "h3",
            "h4",
            "h5",
            "h6",
            "td",
            "th",
            "pre",
        }:
            if self.current:
                self._finish()
            self.current = {"tag": tag, "parts": [], "link_chars": 0}

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
            return
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a" and self.link_depth:
            self.link_depth -= 1
        if self.current and tag == self.current["tag"]:
            self._finish()

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth or not self.current:
            return
        self.current["parts"].append(data)
        if self.link_depth:
            self.current["link_chars"] += len(data)

    def close(self):
        super().close()
        if self.current:
            self._finish()

    def _finish(self):
        text = _html_normalize("".join(self.current["parts"]))
        if text:
            self.blocks.append(
                {
                    "text": text,
                    "link_ratio": self.current["link_chars"]
                    / max(1, len(text)),
                }
            )
        self.current = None

class _HtmlSemanticCollector(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.candidates = []
        self.stack = []
        self.link_depth = 0
        self.skip_depth = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a":
            self.link_depth += 1
        if tag in {"article", "main", "section", "div", "body"}:
            attr_map = dict(attrs)
            marker = " ".join(
                (attr_map.get("id", ""), attr_map.get("class", ""))
            ).lower()
            self.stack.append(
                {
                    "tag": tag,
                    "marker": marker,
                    "parts": [],
                    "link_chars": 0,
                }
            )

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
            return
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a" and self.link_depth:
            self.link_depth -= 1
        if self.stack and tag == self.stack[-1]["tag"]:
            candidate = self.stack.pop()
            text = _html_normalize("".join(candidate["parts"]))
            if text:
                bonus = (
                    1200
                    if candidate["tag"] == "article"
                    else 900
                    if candidate["tag"] == "main"
                    else 0
                )
                if any(
                    key in candidate["marker"]
                    for key in (
                        "article",
                        "content",
                        "main",
                        "post",
                        "story",
                    )
                ):
                    bonus += 600
                penalty = candidate["link_chars"] * 4
                self.candidates.append(
                    {"text": text, "score": len(text) + bonus - penalty}
                )

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        for candidate in self.stack:
            candidate["parts"].append(data)
            if self.link_depth:
                candidate["link_chars"] += len(data)

def _html_residual_extract(value):
    renderer = _HtmlTextRenderer(layout=False)
    renderer.feed(value)
    renderer.close()
    return renderer.render(), {"tag_events": renderer.tag_count}

def _html_layout_extract(value):
    renderer = _HtmlTextRenderer(layout=True)
    renderer.feed(value)
    renderer.close()
    return renderer.render(), {"tag_events": renderer.tag_count}

def _html_block_density_extract(value):
    parser = _HtmlBlockCollector()
    parser.feed(value)
    parser.close()
    selected = [
        block["text"]
        for block in parser.blocks
        if len(block["text"]) >= 80 and block["link_ratio"] <= 0.30
    ]
    if not selected:
        selected = [
            block["text"]
            for block in sorted(
                parser.blocks,
                key=lambda item: len(item["text"]),
                reverse=True,
            )[:3]
        ]
    return "\n\n".join(selected), {
        "candidate_blocks": len(parser.blocks),
        "selected_blocks": len(selected),
    }

def _html_semantic_extract(value):
    parser = _HtmlSemanticCollector()
    parser.feed(value)
    parser.close()
    if not parser.candidates:
        return _html_residual_extract(value)
    best = max(parser.candidates, key=lambda item: item["score"])
    return best["text"], {
        "candidate_nodes": len(parser.candidates),
        "best_score": round(best["score"], 2),
    }

def _html_jsonld_extract(value):
    matches = _html_re.findall(
        r'(?is)<script[^>]+type=["\']application/ld\+json["\'][^>]*>(.*?)</script>',
        value,
    )
    values = []
    parsed = 0
    for payload in matches:
        try:
            item = _html_json.loads(payload)
        except _html_json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        parsed += 1
        nodes = (
            item
            if isinstance(item, list)
            else item.get("@graph", [item])
            if isinstance(item, dict)
            else []
        )
        for node in nodes:
            if isinstance(node, dict):
                for key in (
                    "headline",
                    "name",
                    "description",
                    "articleBody",
                ):
                    item_value = node.get(key)
                    if isinstance(item_value, str):
                        values.append(item_value)
    return _html_normalize(" ".join(values)), {
        "jsonld_scripts": len(matches),
        "jsonld_parsed": parsed,
    }

def _html_load_or_cache(target_documents):
    HTML_EVAL_ROOT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    records = []
    if HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.exists():
        with HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            for line in handle:
                if line.strip():
                    records.append(_html_json.loads(line))
        if len(records) >= target_documents:
            return records[:target_documents], "cache"
    from datasets import load_dataset

    records = []
    skipped_oversized = 0
    stream = load_dataset(
        HTML_EVAL_DATASET,
        split=HTML_EVAL_SPLIT,
        streaming=True,
        revision=HTML_EVAL_REVISION,
    )
    with HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for source_index, source in enumerate(stream):
            html = source.get("html") or ""
            if not html or len(html) > _HTML_EVAL_MAX_CHARS:
                skipped_oversized += 1
                continue
            record = {
                "source_index": source_index,
                "c4_shard": source.get("c4_shard"),
                "timestamp": source.get("c4_timestamp"),
                "url": source.get("url"),
                "html": html,
                "reference_text": source.get("text") or "",
            }
            handle.write(
                _html_json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n"
            )
            records.append(record)
            if len(records) >= target_documents:
                break
    HTML_EVAL_MANIFEST_PATH.write_text(
        _html_json.dumps(
            {
                "dataset": HTML_EVAL_DATASET,
                "revision": HTML_EVAL_REVISION,
                "split": HTML_EVAL_SPLIT,
                "selection": "first sequential non-empty HTML records under 500,000 characters",
                "requested_documents": target_documents,
                "retained_documents": len(records),
                "skipped_oversized_or_empty": skipped_oversized,
                "raw_path": str(HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH),
            },
            ensure_ascii=False,
            indent=2,
        ),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    return records, "stream"

def run_html_technique_evaluation(target_documents):
    records, selection_source = _html_load_or_cache(target_documents)
    techniques = [
        (
            "residual_markup",
            "Residual markup removal",
            "Transparent HTMLParser baseline",
            _html_residual_extract,
            "main-content baseline",
        ),
        (
            "block_density",
            "Block-density selection",
            "jusText-style local proxy",
            _html_block_density_extract,
            "main-content candidate",
        ),
        (
            "semantic_dom",
            "Semantic DOM scoring",
            "Readability/Trafilatura-family local proxy",
            _html_semantic_extract,
            "main-content candidate",
        ),
        (
            "layout_renderer",
            "Layout-preserving rendering",
            "Inscriptis-style local proxy",
            _html_layout_extract,
            "layout-preserving text",
        ),
        (
            "jsonld_metadata",
            "Structured metadata extraction",
            "extruct-style JSON-LD proxy",
            _html_jsonld_extract,
            "metadata only",
        ),
    ]
    aggregate = {
        key: {
            "documents": 0,
            "nonempty": 0,
            "output_characters": 0,
            "overlap_sum": 0.0,
            "signals": _HtmlCounter(),
        }
        for key, *_ in techniques
    }
    raw_html_characters = 0
    reference_characters = 0
    document_rows = []
    with HTML_EVAL_DOCUMENT_METRICS_PATH.open(
        "w", encoding="utf-8"
    ) as output:
        for record in records:
            raw_html_characters += len(record["html"])
            reference_characters += len(record["reference_text"])
            document_metrics = {
                "source_index": record["source_index"],
                "url": record["url"],
                "raw_html_characters": len(record["html"]),
                "reference_characters": len(record["reference_text"]),
                "techniques": {},
            }
            for key, _, _, extractor, _ in techniques:
                extracted, signals = extractor(record["html"])
                overlap = _html_overlap(
                    extracted, record["reference_text"]
                )
                stats = aggregate[key]
                stats["documents"] += 1
                stats["nonempty"] += bool(extracted)
                stats["output_characters"] += len(extracted)
                stats["overlap_sum"] += overlap
                stats["signals"].update(signals)
                document_metrics["techniques"][key] = {
                    "output_characters": len(extracted),
                    "reference_token_overlap": round(overlap, 6),
                    "signals": signals,
                }
            output.write(
                _html_json.dumps(document_metrics, ensure_ascii=False)
                + "\n"
            )
    metrics = []
    for key, name, implementation, _, role in techniques:
        stats = aggregate[key]
        metrics.append(
            {
                "technique": name,
                "implementation": implementation,
                "role": role,
                "status": "executed",
                "documents": stats["documents"],
                "nonempty_rate": round(
                    100 * stats["nonempty"] / max(1, stats["documents"]), 2
                ),
                "mean_output_characters": round(
                    stats["output_characters"]
                    / max(1, stats["documents"]),
                    1,
                ),
                "output_vs_html_percent": round(
                    100
                    * stats["output_characters"]
                    / max(1, raw_html_characters),
                    3,
                ),
                "mean_reference_token_overlap_percent": round(
                    100
                    * stats["overlap_sum"]
                    / max(1, stats["documents"]),
                    2,
                ),
                "aggregate_signals": dict(stats["signals"]),
            }
        )
    for library, available in _HTML_EVAL_LIBRARY_STATUS.items():
        if not available:
            metrics.append(
                {
                    "technique": library,
                    "implementation": "External library adapter",
                    "role": "library implementation",
                    "status": "not executed: dependency unavailable in active kernel",
                    "documents": 0,
                    "nonempty_rate": None,
                    "mean_output_characters": None,
                    "output_vs_html_percent": None,
                    "mean_reference_token_overlap_percent": None,
                    "aggregate_signals": {},
                }
            )
    metrics.extend(
        [
            {
                "technique": "MinerU-HTML / AICC",
                "implementation": "Learned HTML sequence-labeling model",
                "role": "model-based main-content extraction",
                "status": "not executed: model/runtime unavailable; no Hindi validation claim",
                "documents": 0,
                "nonempty_rate": None,
                "mean_output_characters": None,
                "output_vs_html_percent": None,
                "mean_reference_token_overlap_percent": None,
                "aggregate_signals": {},
            },
            {
                "technique": "SCRIBES",
                "implementation": "Per-site semi-structured script generation",
                "role": "site-specific structured extraction",
                "status": "not executed: no runtime; requires same-site page groups",
                "documents": 0,
                "nonempty_rate": None,
                "mean_output_characters": None,
                "output_vs_html_percent": None,
                "mean_reference_token_overlap_percent": None,
                "aggregate_signals": {},
            },
        ]
    )
    result = {
        "dataset": HTML_EVAL_DATASET,
        "revision": HTML_EVAL_REVISION,
        "selection_source": selection_source,
        "documents": len(records),
        "raw_html_characters": raw_html_characters,
        "reference_text_characters": reference_characters,
        "library_status": _HTML_EVAL_LIBRARY_STATUS,
        "metrics": metrics,
        "manifest_path": str(HTML_EVAL_MANIFEST_PATH),
        "metrics_path": str(HTML_EVAL_METRICS_PATH),
        "document_metrics_path": str(HTML_EVAL_DOCUMENT_METRICS_PATH),
    }
    HTML_EVAL_METRICS_PATH.write_text(
        _html_json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    return result

def load_html_technique_evaluation():
    if not HTML_EVAL_METRICS_PATH.exists():
        return None
    return _html_json.loads(
        HTML_EVAL_METRICS_PATH.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    )

# Notebook Improvements

When the user asks to improve, optimize, or clean up their notebook, scan the
current cells for these opportunities. Use your judgment — don't over-apply,
and if you're unsure whether a change is worthwhile, ask the user.

## Cell names

Low priority unless the user asks. `setup` and cells defining
functions/classes are auto-named by marimo. Beyond that, naming is optional.
Note that naming markdown cells clutters the UI by showing the cell header
that's normally hidden.

## Setup cell

A setup cell is named `"setup"` and is guaranteed to run before all other
cells. It's the place for module imports. Consolidating imports here keeps
the notebook clean and ensures every cell can rely on those modules being
available.

**The setup cell cannot reference other cells' variables.** It runs first, so
it must be self-contained: imports, constants, and definitions that depend only
on each other. Reading a name defined elsewhere (e.g. `df`, a UI element) fails
with `The setup cell cannot have references`.

First check if the notebook already has a cell named `"setup"`. If not, create
one and hoist scattered imports into it. `name="setup"` auto-positions the cell
first — no `before`/`after` needed:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell('''import polars as pl
import marimo as mo
import anywidget
import traitlets''', name="setup")
ctx.run_cell(cid)
```

If a setup cell already exists, `create_cell(name="setup")` raises `ValueError`;
use `ctx.edit_cell("setup", code=...)` and `ctx.run_cell("setup")` instead.

## Lift reusable functions into their own cells

When a cell contains a single function or class that doesn't reference
variables from other cells, marimo treats it specially — it can be written as
a standalone definition and reused outside the notebook. These functions can
use modules from the setup cell.

Look for functions that **could belong in a library**: data loading, transforms,
parsers, domain logic, custom widgets. If someone might reasonably `import` it
from another module, it's a good candidate to lift into its own cell.

Don't lift everything — notebook-specific wiring (UI layout, display logic,
cell-level orchestration) should stay where it is. Use `_prefix` for
cell-internal helpers that aren't meant to be reused.

```python
# before: useful logic buried in a larger cell
objects = pl.read_csv("https://example.com/objects.csv")
artists = pl.read_csv("https://example.com/artists.csv")

def top_counts(df, col, n=5):
    return df.group_by(col).len().sort("len", descending=True).head(n)

result = top_counts(objects.join(artists, on="id"), "category")
```

```python
# after: top_counts is general-purpose — give it its own cell

# cell 1
def top_counts(df, col, n=5):
    return df.group_by(col).len().sort("len", descending=True).head(n)
```

```python
# cell 2
result = top_counts(df, "category")
```

## `mo.persistent_cache`

`@mo.persistent_cache` caches a function's result to disk so it isn't
recomputed on subsequent runs. The cache persists across kernel restarts.

```python
@mo.persistent_cache
def load_data():
    objects = pl.read_csv("https://example.com/objects.csv")
    artists = pl.read_csv("https://example.com/artists.csv")
    return objects.join(artists, on="id", how="left")

df = load_data()
```

Good candidates: data loading, ETL, expensive computation that rarely changes.
Don't over-optimize — if you're unsure, suggest it to the user rather than
applying it.

````

```
===== assignment =====
mo.md(r"""
# Session 4 — Dataset Cleaning and Deduplication

## Project specification

This notebook documents a reproducible, evidence-based data-cleaning case study. The selected corpus must contain approximately 10–100 million tokens, undergo the applicable cleaning stages, and be accompanied by an interactive report that records methodology, decisions, and measured outcomes.

## Required pipeline stages

1. Extraction
2. Normalization
3. Language identification and validation
4. Quality filtering
5. Deduplication
6. Personally identifiable information (PII) scrubbing
7. Decontamination
8. Manifest and provenance

## Notebook scope

This notebook implements and evaluates **Stage 1: Extraction** only. Subsequent stages remain separate so that each transformation, metric, and hand-off artifact is independently auditable.
""")
===== dataset_selection =====
mo.md(r"""
# Dataset Selection

| Candidate | Technical assessment |
|---|---|
| Hindi Wikipedia | Within the token target, but insufficient residual cleaning signal for this study. |
| OSCAR Hindi | Suitable raw-web alternative; acquisition and manual review requirements are higher. |
| IndicCorp Hindi | Predominantly short, previously cleaned lines; limited evidence for document-level extraction, deduplication, or PII analysis. |
| xP3 / IndicParaphrase | Instruction/paraphrase records rather than a document-pretraining corpus. |
| **Sangraha verified Hindi** | **Selected.** Open, document-level Hindi corpus with provenance metadata and measurable residual artifacts. |

**Dataset identifier:** `ai4bharat/sangraha` · **configuration:** `verified` · **split:** `hin` · **target:** approximately **30 million estimated tokens**.

**Selection rationale:** The corpus provides document-level Hindi text, source-type metadata, and sufficient residual formatting variation to support a conservative extraction evaluation. The lecture demonstration dataset is not used.
""")
===== html_eval_scope =====
mo.md(r"""
# Auxiliary HTML Extraction Evaluation Corpus

This controlled English-language evaluation is separate from the Hindi Sangraha case study. It uses a bounded, revision-pinned subset of `bs-modeling-metadata/c4-en-html-with-metadata`, which retains raw `html`, `url`, and a supplied `text` field. Its purpose is to execute extraction *families* against real HTML and compare their aggregate behavior.

The supplied C4 `text` field is an **agreement proxy**, not human-labeled ground truth. Token overlap with it measures method disagreement; it does not establish semantic extraction accuracy. A Hindi-literate source-level reference set would still be required before transferring a threshold or quality claim to the Sangraha study.
""")
===== html_eval_controls =====
html_eval_target_documents = mo.ui.slider(
    start=10,
    stop=50,
    step=10,
    value=30,
    label="HTML documents in deterministic evaluation subset",
    show_value=True,
)
run_html_evaluation = mo.ui.run_button(
    label="Download subset and execute HTML extraction comparison"
)
mo.vstack(
    [
        mo.md(
            "The subset is cached under `data/c4_en_html_evaluation/`; raw HTML remains separate from Sangraha. The run writes aggregate metrics and document-level metrics without displaying page text."
        ),
        mo.hstack([html_eval_target_documents, run_html_evaluation]),
    ]
)

````
---
name: marimo-pair
description: >-
  Drive a live marimo notebook as a workspace: run Python in the same kernel
  the user does, inspect live notebook state, and commit durable notebook
  changes. Use when the user wants to start a marimo notebook or pair on an
  active marimo session.
allowed-tools: Bash(bash **/scripts/discover-servers.sh *), Bash(bash **/scripts/execute-code.sh *), Read
---

marimo is a reactive Python runtime for building reproducible Python programs
(marimo notebooks). Cells are connected by the variables they define and
reference. Running a cell re-executes dependents in dataflow order. The active
runtime holds the kernel namespace, cell state, and dataflow graph. The
notebook (`.py` file) is the artifact the kernel writes from that state while a
session is running.

A user interacts with the same runtime via a notebook UI with cells, outputs,
and widgets.

**WARNING. The active runtime is the source of truth.** During a session, you
SHOULD NOT modify the associated `.py` file directly. File edits WILL NOT reach
the active kernel or user, and the kernel may overwrite them on save. Use
`marimo._code_mode` (`cm`) for notebook changes. Reading disk is fine, but
prefer `ctx.cells[...].code` for current cell code.

## Connect to a Notebook

Use the bundled script (`bash scripts/execute-code.sh`) or MCP
(`execute_code(...)`) to run Python in a live marimo kernel.

If the user provides a notebook URL, target it directly:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 -c "print('connected')"
```

Use `-c` only for short one-liners. For multiline code or code containing
quotes, backticks, `$`, or braces, use a single-quoted heredoc:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 <<'PY'
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
PY
```

When code already lives in a file, pass the file path:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 /tmp/code.py
```

If no target is provided, find or start a session. First look for a running
session with `bash scripts/discover-servers.sh`, MCP `list_sessions()`, or
local process context. When multiple sessions are possible, target with
`--url`, `--port`, or `--session`.

If no server is running and the user wants a notebook, start marimo with
`--no-token` (and without `--headless`) so it auto-registers for discovery. The
notebook UI must be open before there is an active session for `execute-code`
to target. The right way to invoke marimo depends on context (project tooling,
global install, sandbox mode). If the notebook file contains a PEP 723 `#
/// script` header, it MUST be opened with `--sandbox` — otherwise marimo
ignores the inline dependencies. See
[finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) for the full decision tree and
[execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) for scripts, MCP, and
shell quoting.

## Scratchpad Scope

`execute-code` evaluates Python in marimo's scratchpad: a temporary namespace
with a shallow copy of the kernel globals. Notebook variables are available by
name, but new top-level bindings and rebindings are discarded after each call.
In-place mutations to notebook-owned objects can persist because those names
still reference live objects.

Each call reports stdout and stderr from the scratchpad, plus console output
from notebook cells it causes to run, including reactive descendants.

### Ordinary Python

Use ordinary Python in the scratchpad to inspect variables, sample data, test
transformations, probe APIs, check imports, and read widget state.

```python
print(df.head())

x = 10
print(x)
```

Here `df` comes from notebook globals, while `x` is a scratchpad-local binding.
`x` exists for this call only and WILL NOT be added to notebook globals.

### Persist with `cm`

Top-level scratchpad assignments and rebindings are temporary. To persist work,
including new variables, you MUST submit changes through `marimo._code_mode`
(`cm`).

`marimo._code_mode` is a PRIVATE, UNSTABLE agent API (note the leading
underscore). It exists for tools like this skill to drive a live kernel from
the scratchpad. DO NOT import it from notebook cells, library code, or
anything a user would run — methods can change or disappear across marimo
versions and kernels. Treat every `import marimo._code_mode as cm` as
scratchpad-only.

At session start, inspect what `cm` exposes in the active kernel:

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

help(cm)
```

Open a code-mode context to queue notebook changes.

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
```

The scratchpad supports top-level async code. Use `async with` directly;
wrapping it in `asyncio.run(...)` is unnecessary and can conflict with the
kernel's event loop.

After this block exits and the new cell runs, `x` is notebook state. Later
scratchpad calls can read `x` by name. Code later in the same scratchpad call
should read `ctx.globals["x"]`, because the scratchpad namespace was copied
before the cell ran.

Inside the context, queued mutation methods are synchronous. Call them
directly; do not `await` them. Each call queues an operation for marimo to
apply when the context exits normally. If the block raises, the queue is
discarded.

On clean exit, marimo applies packages, validates and applies structural cell
changes, runs queued cells, then may run dependents. Validation is only
structural since queued cell runs can still error. `create_cell` and
`edit_cell` change notebook structure only. Use `run_cell` to execute. 

`create_cell` currently defaults to `hide_code=True`, which collapses the code
editor in the UI. Pass `hide_code=False` if the user wants created cells to
be visible without manually expanding them.


## Marimo Rules

marimo imposes a small contract on notebook code so it can keep the notebook as
a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

- **No cycles** - cells cannot depend on each other in a cycle.
- **No public redefinitions across cells** - each name has one owning cell.
- **No wildcard imports** - `import *` prevents static analysis of definitions.

These rules keep the kernel, UI, and saved artifact consistent.

When `cm` submits a cell body, marimo parses its top-level definitions and
references. A top-level name enters the graph unless it is private with a
leading underscore.

```python
# Public definitions: values, total, i, value, mean
values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
total = 0
for i, value in enumerate(values):
    total += value
mean = total / len(values)
mean
```

```python
# Public definition: mean
_values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
_total = 0
for _i, _value in enumerate(_values):
    _total += _value
mean = _total / len(_values)
mean
```

Use private names for intermediates that no other cell should read. Public
names define the notebook-level dataflow. If a `cm` edit violates the contract,
marimo rejects the structural change and returns the validation error.

## The Notebook's Shape

A notebook is an ordered collection of cells. `ctx.cells` is the document view
and `ctx.graph` is the dataflow view.

```python
for cell in ctx.cells:
    cell  # .id, .code, .name, .config, .status, .errors

ctx.cells["setup"]         # by name
ctx.cells[0]               # by position
list(ctx.cells.keys())     # all IDs, in notebook order
```

Cell IDs are opaque strings which can be queried from the notebook or captured
from `cm` return values:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell("df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')")
print(cid)   # e.g. 'Hbol'
```

Alternatively, cells can be assigned and referenced by `name`. The graph can be
used to understand its role in the dataflow.

```python
for cid, impl in ctx.graph.cells.items():
    impl  # .defs, .refs   (sets of public names)

ctx.graph.descendants(cid)   # cells that re-run when this one changes
ctx.graph.ancestors(cid)     # cells this one depends on
```

In marimo, deletes are *destructive* so it can be useful to query the
descendants prior to deleting to understand it's impact.

## Writing Notebook Changes

The graph contract keeps marimo able to run and save the notebook. Passing
those checks alone does not guarantee a useful artifact. Committed cells should
still be readable, rerunnable, and editable.

Make durable edits that reuse the notebook's existing names, imports,
dependencies, and UI model. Don't be lazy. Avoid one-off workarounds that pass
`cm` validation but leave a brittle notebook.

### Cell Bodies

Submit the code that belongs in the cell.

- **Submit cell contents** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` take cell contents,
  not saved-file `@app.cell` wrappers.
- **Read before replacing** - for now, another editor may change a cell between
  scratchpad calls. Before `edit_cell`, read the current body from
  `ctx.cells[...]` and submit the full replacement.
- **Reuse notebook imports** - if `np` already exists, use it or edit the owning
  import cell. DO NOT add `import numpy as _np` just to bypass the graph.
- **Define public names intentionally** - use public names for values later
  cells should reference. Use private `_name` bindings or function locals for
  same-cell intermediates.
- **Define each public name once** - a public name has one owning cell.
  Reassigning it in another cell fails with `Multiply-defined names`; edit the
  owning cell or give the result a new name. See
  [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md).
- **Run cells deliberately** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` change structure
  only. Queue `ctx.run_cell(...)` when the cell should execute.

### Prefer `cm`-Managed Changes

Use `cm` APIs when they exist. Avoid direct file edits, shell package commands,
and scratchpad-only state for changes that should persist.

- **Do not edit the `.py` artifact** - DO NOT use `Edit`, `Write`, or
  `NotebookEdit` on the notebook file during a live session. Use
  `ctx.edit_cell(...)` even for small changes.
- **Manage packages through `cm`** - use `ctx.packages.add()` or
  `ctx.packages.remove()` instead of direct `uv` or `pip`; confirm
  non-obvious dependency changes.
- **Avoid transient paths** - persisted cells should not depend on `/tmp/...`
  unless the work is intentionally transient.
- **Delete deliberately** - deleting a cell removes globals it defines. Reuse
  empty cells when convenient and delete cells left empty after edits.

### UI and Widgets

Inspect the object before changing it. Different UI objects update through
different paths.

- **Set `mo.ui.*` through `cm`** - use `ctx.set_ui_value(element, value)` inside
  `cm.get_context()`.
- **Set anywidget traitlets directly** - synced traitlets are Python
  attributes, for example `widget.value = 5`.

For designing custom visual or interactive output, see
[rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md).

## References

- [execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) — scripts, MCP, auth, startup, and shell quoting
- [finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) — choosing the right marimo invocation
- [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md) — name redefinition, cached module proxies, and notebook traps
- [rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md) — custom widgets and visualizations
- [notebook-improvements.md](reference/notebook-improvements.md) — improving existing notebooks

It is designed to keep the page’s article-like content while discarding common surrounding material such as navigation, sidebars, cookie notices, related-link clusters, and repeated template text.\n\n### How it works under the hood\n1. Parses the raw HTML into a document tree.\n2. Removes or deprioritizes elements that are structurally likely to be non-content.\n3. Evaluates remaining text-bearing elements with structural, textual, and link-related signals.\n4. Assembles the selected elements into text, with optional tables, links, metadata, and comments controlled by parameters.\n\n### Use it when\nUse Trafilatura as a strong general-purpose baseline for article/news/blog extraction when raw HTML and the page URL are retained. It is appropriate when output should favor readable prose over preserving every page element.\n\n### Advantages\n- Mature, configurable article-extraction workflow.\n- Good default comparison point for raw web pages.\n- Can include or exclude comments, tables, links, metadata, and duplicate text deliberately.\n\n### Limitations and failure modes\n- A page with several similarly dense regions can select the wrong one.\n- Non-article pages, short pages, product pages, and custom site templates need review.\n- High retained-text overlap does not prove that boilerplate was removed correctly.\n\n### Notebook note\nThis run uses `include_comments=False`, keeps tables, and records only aggregate measurements. For Hindi deployment, build source-page labels first; do not transfer this English-C4 result or its defaults as a Hindi quality threshold.''',\n    'justext': r'''## jusText — block-level boilerplate classification\n\n### What it does\njusText separates page text into blocks, then classifies each block as content or boilerplate. It is aimed at removing menus, repeated navigation, link lists, and template fragments without needing a site-specific selector.\n\n### How it works under the hood\n1. Parses HTML into paragraph-like text blocks.\n2. Computes block properties such as length, link density, stopword density, and paragraph structure.\n3. Marks obvious good and bad blocks.\n4. Revises ambiguous blocks by looking at neighboring blocks, which prevents isolated short content fragments from being discarded too eagerly.\n\n### Use it when\nUse jusText when you want an interpretable, block-level baseline for pages with strong navigation and repeated templates. It is useful for diagnosing *why* text was retained or rejected.\n\n### Advantages\n- Decisions are made at paragraph/block level rather than as opaque whole-page selection.\n- Link density makes it useful for menu-heavy pages.\n- The contextual revision step is more robust than a single length cutoff.\n\n### Limitations and failure modes\n- Stopword and whitespace assumptions are language-sensitive.\n- Headings, short notices, verse, captions, and lists can resemble boilerplate.\n- It extracts prose blocks; it is not a layout-preserving converter.\n\n### Notebook note\nThe executable auxiliary corpus is English, so this call uses jusText’s English stoplist. That is intentional for this comparison and must not be copied to Hindi/Hinglish data without a Hindi-literate error analysis.''',\n    'inscriptis': r'''## Inscriptis — layout-aware HTML-to-text rendering\n\n### What it does\nInscriptis converts HTML to readable text while preserving useful display boundaries. Parses HTML and walks the document structure.\n2. Applies rendering rules for block elements, line breaks, lists, tables, and other layout-relevant tags.\n3. Omits scripts/styles and emits text with structural spacing instead of naïvely concatenating every text node.\n4. Pair it with a boilerplate/main-content method when the training corpus requires only central prose.''',\n    'resiliparse': r'''## Resiliparse — high-throughput HTML text extraction\n\n### What it does\nResiliparse provides an optimized HTML parsing and text-extraction path for crawl-scale pipelines. It is useful when raw HTML must be processed quickly while preserving a source-artifact-first workflow.\n\n### How it works under the hood\n1. Parses raw HTML with an optimized DOM implementation.\n2. Traverses the DOM and removes excluded or non-textual elements.\n3. Applies its main-content extraction mode to focus the text result.\n4. Emits plain text with optional formatting, links, comments, and metadata behavior controlled by the extraction call.\n\n### Use it when\nUse Resiliparse for large HTML/WARC collections where parse throughput and memory behavior matter, and where every output can still be traced to the original response.\n\n### Advantages\n- Designed for high-volume web processing.\n- Fits streaming source → extract → record pipelines.\n- Lets a pipeline separate throughput benchmarking from content-quality evaluation.\n\n### Limitations and failure modes\n- Fast parsing does not solve article-boundary ambiguity.\n- Main-content heuristics can still fail on unusual templates or semi-structured pages.\n- Runtime speed and retained character count are not quality metrics.\n\n### Notebook note\nThis notebook calls `extract_plain_text(..., main_content=True)` and preserves formatting. Before using it for a corpus decision, measure domain-stratified precision, false deletions, throughput, and memory independently.''',\n    'readability': r'''## readability-lxml — article-candidate scoring\n\n### What it does\nreadability-lxml is a Python implementation of the Readability-style approach: it seeks one DOM container that most resembles the page’s primary article, then returns that candidate’s HTML/text.\n\n### How it works under the hood\n1. Parses the HTML with lxml.\n2. Scores candidate containers using text volume, link-heavy content, and article-like or boilerplate-like structural markers.\n3. Selects the highest-scoring candidate as the probable main article.\n4. Produces cleaned candidate HTML; this notebook then renders that HTML into text for measurement.\n\n### Use it when\nUse readability-lxml for conventional article/news/blog pages where one main content container is expected and you want a compact, readable baseline.\n\n### Advantages\n- Simple single-article selection model.\n- Often effective for editorial web pages with a clear article body.\n- Useful comparator against multi-signal tools such as Trafilatura.\n\n### Limitations and failure modes\n- A single winning container is a poor fit for forums, search pages, catalogs, dashboards, and multi-article pages.\n- Short content, image-led pages, and tables can be under-selected.\n- CSS class/id hints are heuristic; site conventions are not universal.\n\n### Notebook note\nThe code explicitly renders Readability’s selected HTML through the same residual renderer used for a control, so the measured difference reflects candidate selection rather than two unrelated text serializers.''',\n    'extruct': r'''## extruct — structured metadata extraction\n\n### What it does\nextruct extracts machine-readable metadata embedded in HTML. Decodes formats such as JSON-LD, Microdata, RDFa, Open Graph, or microformats when requested.\n3. Returns structured Python records rather than a page-text candidate.\n4. A caller chooses which fields—such as `headline`, `description`, or `articleBody`—are useful for its policy.\n\n### Use it when\nUse extruct when you need publisher-provided titles, dates, authors, canonical metadata, schema types, or a possible article-body field for provenance checks, routing, and validation.\n\n### Advantages\n- Preserves explicit structured fields when publishers expose them.\n- Helpful for source-level provenance and downstream quality checks.\n- Complements prose extractors by providing metadata they may discard.\n\n### Limitations and failure modes\n- Metadata may be missing, stale, incomplete, or inconsistent with visible text.\n- A JSON-LD `articleBody` field is publisher supplied; it is not ground truth.\n- Its output size is not comparable to a main-content extractor.\n\n### Notebook note\nThis executable run intentionally requests **JSON-LD only** and collects a conservative field subset.
